research_question: What are the evidence-based principles of conversion-focused visual hierarchy for a landing/marketing page — above-the-fold value proposition, a single dominant CTA, hook->proof->CTA flow, and elimination of competing focal points — and which of these can be expressed as mechanically-checkable rules for an AI web-conversion designer building Next.js + Tailwind pages?

phases.name: Landscape
phases.objective: Survey the anatomy of a high-converting landing page: the one-page-one-goal principle, above-the-fold value proposition, the message-match / attention-ratio concept (1:1), and the hook->proof->CTA narrative structure.
sub_questions: What does conversion research (CXL, NN/g, Unbounce-style attention-ratio) say is the canonical structure and section order of a high-converting page?
What belongs above the fold and how does 'the fold' still matter given scroll behavior?
phases.evidence_priorities: CXL landing-page anatomy + above-the-fold articles, NN/g scanning/F-pattern research, attention-ratio concept, value-proposition frameworks.
phases.stop_condition: Complete when the canonical section model and the above-the-fold requirement set are enumerated with evidence.

phases.name: Mechanics
phases.objective: How dominant-CTA hierarchy is built: one primary CTA repeated at decision points, visual weight via size/color/contrast/whitespace/isolation, directional cues, Von Restorff (isolation effect) and Serial-Position (primacy/recency), F- and Z- scanning patterns, and 'every element installs a belief or removes an objection.'
sub_questions: What concrete visual techniques make one CTA unmissable and how do you measure 'one dominant focal point'?
How do serial-position and isolation effects dictate placement of the value prop, CTA, and proof?
phases.evidence_priorities: Laws of UX (Von Restorff, Serial Position), CXL CTA/button research, eye-tracking studies, color-contrast-for-emphasis (not a11y) literature.
phases.stop_condition: Complete when CTA-dominance and focal-point techniques are expressed as measurable layout assertions.

phases.name: Failure Modes
phases.objective: Conversion-killing hierarchy defects: multiple competing CTAs of equal weight, high attention-ratio (many nav links/links competing with the goal), buried or vague value prop, hero with no clear next action, low-contrast 'ghost' primary buttons, decorative imagery that out-weighs the message, slow/heavy hero, generic headline that states category not benefit.
sub_questions: Which hierarchy mistakes most reduce conversion in documented tests/case studies?
How does each defect read to a first-time visitor scanning for 3-5 seconds?
phases.evidence_priorities: CXL/landing-page teardown case studies, A/B-test write-ups, attention-ratio data, NN/g 'banner blindness' and scanning.
phases.stop_condition: Complete when 8+ distinct conversion-hierarchy defects are documented with mechanism and detection signal.

phases.name: Contrarian
phases.objective: Where conversion-hierarchy dogma is wrong or overstated: 'the fold is dead' debate vs real scroll data; long-form vs short-form; when multiple CTAs are legitimate (different intents); benefit-vs-clarity tension; honest hierarchy vs manipulative urgency (links to ethics/dark patterns).
sub_questions: What is the strongest evidence against the single-CTA / above-the-fold orthodoxy?
Where does aggressive conversion hierarchy cross into deceptive design?
phases.evidence_priorities: Scroll-behavior studies, 'fold is dead' analyses, deceptive.design overlap, contrarian CRO writers.
phases.stop_condition: Complete when 2+ substantive counter-arguments are documented with evidence.

openai_instructions: Build a fault-tree of conversion-hierarchy failure: for a page with a goal, deduce the layout invariants that maximize a single focal path (value prop -> proof -> CTA). Enumerate measurable assertions (one dominant CTA, attention ratio, contrast-for-emphasis, above-fold value prop) and the conditions under which each is violated. Ground emphasis-contrast and serial-position/isolation claims in evidence.
